newsitem.title: USA: Judge upholds New England milk price plan.
newsitem.headline: Judge upholds New England milk price plan.

text.p: U.S. District Judge Paul Friedman on Wednesday upheld a plan allowing New England states to set higher milk prices beginning July 1.
Congress gave the Department of Agriculture the authority, as part of the 1996 Farm Bill, to allow the Northeast Dairy Compact if "it found a compelling public interest."
However, the plan remains controversial, especially with Midwestern dairy producers.
The compact empowers a commission representing the six New England states to adjust the price of milk bound for grocery stores. It can raise prices by up to 25 percent, if desired.
The Milk Industry Foundation filed suit against the pact last year on the grounds that Congress acted unconstitutionally in delegating power for authorizing the pact to USDA.
The MIF further argued that USDA failed to demonstrate a compelling public interest for the arrangement.
In a prepared statement, the MIF expressed disappointment with the decision and said they would take the case to the Federal Court of Appeals.
Not surprisingly, a USDA spokesman hailed the decision.
"We said all along that the compact is valid and we're glad to see that the court agrees with us. However, we will continue to monitor the compact," the spokesman said.
Wisconsin Senators Herb Kohl and Russ Feingold, both Democrats, vowed to work for repeal of the compact.
"The compact is patently unfair to Wisconsin producers" because it increases the "price discrimination they face under the antiquated Federal Milk Marketing Order System," they said.
Meanwhile, several southern states have expressed interest in forming their own dairy compact.
